conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the neurology team. You’re here for your 18th cycle of high-dose methotrexate for your CNS lymphoma, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I just got back from vacation with my husband, so I’m feeling pretty good today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll make sure this cycle goes smoothly. We’ll start with some baseline labs and then give the methotrexate infusion this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Do I need to do anything special before the infusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start IV fluids to help protect your kidneys and give you some anti-nausea meds beforehand. We also give sodium bicarbonate to help clear the methotrexate faster.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin? When does that start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly 24 hours after the methotrexate starts. It helps protect your healthy cells. We’ll monitor your levels daily until they drop low enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Last time my liver enzymes went up a little. Is that expected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, mild elevation is common and usually temporary. We’ll keep an eye on it, but it’s not a concern unless it gets much higher.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. My foot pain has been bothering me more lately. Could that be from the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but we’ve done MRIs and ultrasounds and haven’t found a clear cause. It may not be directly related. We’ll keep you on gabapentin and oxycodone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking the gabapentin regularly. It helps a little, but not completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your primary care doctor knows so they can look into it further. Maybe a pain specialist can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infusion is starting now. It’ll take a few hours. You should feel fine—most people don’t have immediate side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I brought a book, so I’ll just relax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Halfway through the infusion. Any nausea or headache?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel okay. Just a little tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is complete. Great job. We’ll keep the IV fluids going and check your labs tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I expect to feel different tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people feel a bit fatigued or have mild nausea, but we’ll give you meds if needed. The key is staying hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are back. Your methotrexate level is 0.21, which is where we want it. Kidney and liver values are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Does that mean I’m on track to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once it drops below 0.2, you can go home. We’ll check again tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the brain MRI I had yesterday—any results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I just got the report. No new lesions or signs of lymphoma recurrence. Everything looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s such a relief. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good news. We also saw some chronic sinus inflammation, but that’s not new and doesn’t need treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot—why did we stop my aspirin again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because aspirin can interfere with methotrexate clearance. We hold it during the cycle to protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, and I can restart it when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll write that order. You’ve been on it for your history of DVT and PE, so it’s important to continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s just temporary. I worry about clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. But your risk is low now, especially with the aspirin back on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level is now 0.07—excellent. That means you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Do I need to take extra leucovorin or sodium bicarbonate at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, because your level is so low. Just continue your regular meds and stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my citalopram—I should keep taking that every day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. You’ve been doing well emotionally, and we want to keep it that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than I did a few cycles ago. I was really overwhelmed then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a lot to go through. But you’re handling it well now, and your mood is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the next steps with my oncologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dr. ___ plans to start you on Rituxan after this cycle. You’ll discuss that at your next clinic visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that another chemo drug?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a targeted therapy—works with your immune system. It’s often used with methotrexate for lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll ask about it then. And my foot pain—I should see my PCP about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please do. It’s not clearly related to chemo, so your doctor might refer you to a specialist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make an appointment. I just want to walk more without pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll include that in your discharge instructions. Otherwise, you’re doing very well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are in. You can go home in about an hour. Just sign the papers and get your prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and see you at your next cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. No nausea or headaches. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vitals are stable. Your hemoglobin is a bit low, but that’s expected from chemo. No anemia symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little tired sometimes, but nothing severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. Keep eating well and resting. We’ll monitor it next cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my asthma has been fine. I’ve been using my inhalers as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. No wheezing or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, all clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home. Take it easy for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re leaving now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the cab is here. I’m all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels. Call if you have any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.
